title: Maimonides' middle way
hookLine: virtue lies in the middle between extremes
carry: the middle path is the way of the lord

cards: Somewhere between the person who won't pick up the check and the person who hands out money until there's none left for rent, there's a third person. Generous. Not stingy, not wasteful.
Somewhere between the one who freezes at every risk and the one who jumps at all of them, there's another. Brave. Maimonides noticed that good traits seem to live in between.
He wrote it in the Eight Chapters, and again in his code of law. Today, the place in between.

teach.h: TWO EXTREMES, AND THE MEASURE BETWEEN.
teach.b: The middle way. Start with the rule. For almost every trait, Maimonides says, there are two extremes, and both are unhealthy.
The good path is the measure in the middle. Not too much, not too little: generous between stingy and wasteful, brave between reckless and timid, content between greedy and careless.
Second, he gives this path a name from the Torah.

In Genesis, God says Abraham will teach his household to "keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice." Maimonides reads the way of the LORD as this middle path. Walking it is a way of walking in God's ways.

teach.h: TO CURE, LEAN THE OTHER WAY.
teach.b: Third, the cure. If someone has drifted to one extreme, aiming straight for the middle isn't enough. A stingy person, he says, should give generously for a while, even too generously, until the stinginess loosens.
Then come back to the middle. A tree bent one way is pulled the other way before it stands straight. Fourth, the warning.

Some people, wary of desire, swing to the far opposite: refusing ordinary food and comfort, more than the Torah asks. Maimonides calls that a wrong road too. The Torah, he says, didn't forbid ordinary good things.
So the middle isn't lukewarm. It's balanced, and it takes work to stay there, like standing on a moving deck. The middle way.

how: Jewish teachers of character, in the tradition called mussar, study Maimonides' Laws of Character Traits and the Eight Chapters, and students often work on one trait at a time.

o: good traits sit between two unhealthy extremes
never take a firm side in any argument
always choose the safest, least risky option

games.q: the middle way — tap the pairs.
p: Maimonides' name for the middle path

s: Maimonides says the holiest path is refusing all comfort
he calls that extreme a wrong road too; the Torah didn't forbid ordinary good things.
he connects the middle path to a verse about Abraham
Genesis says Abraham's household will keep the way of the LORD.
to fix an extreme, he says to aim straight for the middle
he says to lean to the other side for a while, then return to the middle.

games.q: you've been stingy for years and want to change. what does Maimonides prescribe?
o: aim exactly for the middle, starting today.
give generously for a while, even too much, then settle in the middle.
games.why: he says to lean toward the opposite extreme for a time, until the old trait loosens, then return to the middle.

practice: Choose one ordinary habit, how much you eat, work, talk, or check your phone, and ask which way it leans: too much, or too little? Then picture the middle, not perfect, just balanced, in an actual hour of tomorrow.

wordCard.voice: The middle way. Maimonides' teaching that good traits lie between two extremes, which he calls walking in the way of the LORD. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the way of God (literally, of the Name), Maimonides' name for the middle path.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle path is the way of the LORD. For Maimonides, balanced isn't lukewarm, and holiness doesn't require misery. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.q: keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice
